summary.text: Escape velocity is the speed an object needs so that, with enough energy, it can reach every distance from a body, out to infinity.
It is more accurately a speed than a velocity because direction does not matter, and it gets smaller the farther you are from the body's center.
From Earth's surface it is 11.186 km/s, but a craft in low Earth orbit already moves at about 7.8 km/s, so it needs far less extra speed.

facts.label: Low orbit speed
facts.value: About 7.8 km/s in low Earth orbit

facts.label: Eastward launch
facts.value: About 10.735 km/s relative to the moving equator

facts.label: Launch site latitudes
facts.value: Cape Canaveral 28°28′ N, French Guiana 5°14′ N

items.prompt: A satellite travels in a steady circular orbit around Earth. Compared with the speed needed to leave Earth's pull for good from that same distance, its speed is...

options.label: Exactly the same, which is why it stays up
Always higher, which keeps it circling
Always lower, at its current distance
Higher when near Earth and lower when far

items.explain: An object in a circular or elliptical orbit always has a speed below the escape speed at its current distance.

items.prompt: Two identical rockets leave the equator, one aimed east and one aimed west. Measured against the moving ground, which needs less speed to escape?

options.label: The one aimed east
The one aimed west
Both need exactly the same
Neither could escape from the equator

items.explain: Relative to the rotating surface, the eastward launch needs about 10.735 km/s and the westward launch about 11.665 km/s.

items.prompt: A spacecraft is first parked in a low orbit and then sent on its way, instead of being fired straight from the ground at full speed. Why does this help?

options.label: Gravity switches off once an object is in orbit, so no extra speed is needed
Anything in orbit has an escape speed of zero around Earth
The craft gets heavier in orbit, so its engine pushes harder
It already has a lot of orbital speed, so the extra change needed is far smaller

items.explain: In low Earth orbit the craft already moves at about 7.8 km/s, so the additional change in speed is far less than starting from rest.

items.prompt: A probe is on a parabolic path, always travelling at exactly the speed needed to escape from where it is. What does its speed do over time?

options.label: It stays the same forever
It keeps dropping toward zero but never quite gets there
It reaches zero far away and the probe falls back
It rises steadily as the probe leaves

items.explain: The probe balances positive kinetic energy and negative gravitational potential energy, so it keeps slowing, approaching zero speed but never quite stopping.

items.prompt: Liftoff acceleration and thick air make it hard to reach full escape speed all at once. How can a rocket escape anyway?

options.label: Escape needs less energy if the climb is slow enough
It must still hit the full surface escape speed at some moment
It keeps thrusting, so it can escape at any speed above zero
It cannot escape unless it fires in one single burst

items.explain: A rocket under continuous or intermittent thrust can escape at any non-zero speed, though the minimum energy needed is always the same.

items.prompt: Two small spacecraft of different weights leave Earth. Why can engineers usually ignore which is heavier when working out escape speed?

options.label: Each adds a negligible amount to the combined mass of it and Earth
Gravity pulls every object with the same force, whatever its mass
Air slows heavy craft and not light ones, so the effects cancel
Escape speed depends only on the direction of travel

items.explain: Escape speed depends on the combined mass, but a satellite or small object contributes a negligible part of it, so it is often ignored.
